content.aim: To investigate three discrete-component logic circuits (two diode-resistor circuits and one transistor circuit) and to identify the Boolean function performed by each.
objectives: To construct Circuits A, B and C (Figure 3) using diodes, resistors and an NPN transistor. To measure the output voltage of each circuit for every input combination. To classify each output as logic 0 (0–1 V) or logic 1 (4–5 V). To determine the Boolean function of each circuit and to evaluate what happens if several such circuits are cascaded in series.
apparatus: 1 kΩ resistors (pull-up / pull-down, one per diode circuit)
Low-power silicon diodes (two per diode circuit)

theory.text: Circuit A — Diode AND gate Inputs A and B feed a common node through diodes, with a 1 kΩ resistor pulling the node up to +5 V. If either input is LOW, its diode conducts and clamps the node close to that input's voltage, so the output stays LOW. The output only rises HIGH when both A and B are HIGH (no diode conducts, and the pull-up resistor takes the node to +5 V). This realizes OQ = A AND B. Circuit B — Diode OR gate Inputs A and B feed a common node through diodes, with a 1 kΩ resistor pulling the node down to 0 V. If either input is HIGH, its diode conducts and pulls the node up close to that input's voltage. The output is LOW only when both A and B are LOW. This realizes OQ = A OR B. Circuit C — Transistor inverter (NOT gate) Input A drives the base of an NPN transistor (BC108) through a 10 kΩ resistor; the collector is pulled up to +5 V through 1 kΩ, and the emitter is grounded. When A is HIGH, the transistor saturates and pulls the collector (output) LOW. When A is LOW, the transistor is OFF and the collector is pulled HIGH by the 1 kΩ resistor. This realizes OQ = NOT A.

procedure: Connect each circuit (A, B, C) as shown in Figure 3, using the prototyping board.
Use the voltmeter to measure the output voltage at each circuit's designated output node.
Vary the input(s) through all combinations and complete a truth table for each circuit.
Classify readings of 0–1 V as logic 0 and 4–5 V as logic 1.
precautions: Observe correct diode polarity — a reversed diode will not conduct as intended.
Do not exceed the transistor's maximum collector current or power rating.
Confirm all resistor values with a multimeter before inserting them.
Avoid shorting +5 V directly to ground.
Allow the output to settle before taking each voltmeter reading.
Handle the BC108 transistor by its leads and avoid excessive heat near the package.
content.discussion: The three circuits demonstrate that basic Boolean functions (AND, OR, NOT) can be implemented with discrete diodes and a transistor rather than dedicated logic-gate ICs. Diode gates exploit the one-way conduction of diodes, while the transistor gate uses the switching (saturation/cut-off) behaviour of a BJT to invert and restore the logic level. A practical limitation of diode logic is that each conducting diode introduces a forward voltage drop of approximately 0.6–0.7 V. If several diode gates (Circuits A and/or B) are connected in series without an intervening restoring stage, this drop accumulates: the HIGH level droops and the LOW level rises with each stage. After a few cascaded stages the signal can fall outside the 0–1 V / 4–5 V thresholds used to define logic 0 and 1, causing logic errors. A transistor stage such as Circuit C, which actively switches and restores full-swing output levels, is normally needed between diode-logic stages to prevent this degradation.
content.conclusion: Circuit A implements the AND function, Circuit B implements the OR function, and Circuit C implements the NOT (inverter) function. Diode-resistor logic gates cannot be cascaded indefinitely in series without signal degradation, because of the cumulative diode voltage drop; periodic restoration using an active device (e.g. a transistor stage) is required.
